chunks: Sensing current with MOSFET Vds. The question: How can you use drain-source measurements of a MOSFET to determine current? What are the pros and cons of this setup?
A MOSFET that is fully on behaves like a small resistor, called R DS(on) .
So if you measure the voltage across its two power pins (drain and source) while it conducts, you can compute the current, I equals V DS over R DS(on) .
This adds no extra resistor, no extra loss and no extra parts, which is why it is popular for overcurrent protection.
It is not very accurate, because R DS(on) changes a lot with temperature.
Imagine a pipe that already has a valve in it, and the valve is fully open but still slightly narrow.
You can read the small pressure drop across that valve to estimate the flow, with no new part in the pipe.
The estimate is rough: when the valve warms up it swells and narrows, so the same pressure drop now means less flow.
Also, just after the valve opens the water sloshes, so you wait a moment before trusting the reading.
The comparator's non-inverting input watches the FET's drain; the other input is a threshold.
While the FET is on, V DS = I·R DS(on), so crossing V th means the current exceeded V th/R DS(on). A real design adds blanking, a filter, and a clamp.
R DS(on) : the resistance between drain and source when the FET is fully on. Triode region: the operating region where the FET acts like a resistor.
Blanking time: a short delay after turn-on during which the reading is ignored. Body diode: the diode inside the FET, which can carry current while the FET is off.
Comparator: a circuit that flips its output when a voltage crosses a set threshold.
A FET has R DS(on) equals 5 milliohms at 25 degrees Celsius. At 30 amps the drain-source voltage is 30 times 0. 005 equals 150 millivolts.
Set a comparator at 150 millivolts and it trips at 30 amps when cold. At 125 degrees Celsius the resistance rises by about 1. 68 times, to 8.
4 milliohms, so the same 150 millivolts is reached at only 0. 15 over 0. 0084 equals 17. 8 amps. The threshold slides with temperature. That is the whole idea.
"A fully-on MOSFET is a small resistor, so I equals V DS over R DS(on) .
You measure drain-source voltage with a comparator or amplifier and get current with no added loss, part or board space, which is why it's used for overcurrent protection.

The cons are accuracy: R DS(on) rises 50 percent or more when hot and varies part to part, it only works while the FET is fully on and after the switching edge settles, and the signal is just tens of millivolts.
Good for protection, poor for metering."
